chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Chapter 21 says distraction often wins because the bad default feels cheap in the moment. Skipping the plan, checking the distraction, or drifting off course can look almost free while the real cost stays hidden. That is why Eyal introduces price pacts as a way to attach an explicit consequence before the weak moment begins.

A price pact is a precommitment with a cost. The person decides ahead of time that breaking prior intent will trigger a consequence they chose while thinking clearly. That cost makes the moment less dishonest. The escape route no longer gets to masquerade as painless.

The chapter matters because cost changes the shape of the choice. The person is no longer deciding only between effort and relief. They are also deciding whether to accept a consequence they agreed to earlier.

The sequencing rule stays crucial. Price pacts are not the first answer. They belong after internal-trigger work, traction planning, and external-trigger redesign. If those foundations are missing, the pact can become gimmicky or theatrical instead of useful.

The chapter also keeps a moral boundary. A price pact should protect a genuine value, not become a random act of self-punishment. The cost has to fit the plan it is guarding.

That is why the next chapter can move into identity pacts. Explicit cost is one way to reinforce prior intent; chosen identity becomes another.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Chapter 21 argues that price pacts make distraction less falsely cheap by attaching an explicit cost to breaking the plan. A consequence chosen in advance changes the weak moment so the person is no longer pretending the detour is free.

This matters because many distractions win through cheapness theater. The relief is immediate, while the real cost is delayed or blurry. A price pact corrects that distortion.

The chapter also insists on order. Price pacts come after earlier methods and should protect a real plan rather than substitute for one. Without that sequence, the chapter degrades into gimmicks.

It also avoids punishment rhetoric. The issue is not to suffer dramatically. The issue is to add a consequence that fits the value being protected.

That is why Chapter 22 follows. Once explicit price has been explored, the book can study another pact type that works through chosen identity rather than cost.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Chapter 21 points at one of distraction's dirtiest tricks: the betrayal looks cheap while you're doing it. Skip the block, open the feed, dodge the hard part, and the detour keeps billing itself as basically free. Eyal's answer is to stop accepting fake invoices. A price pact attaches a real cost before the weak moment can start lying.

That matters because the choice changes shape. You are no longer picking only between strain and relief. You are choosing whether to pay a consequence you agreed to when your head was clear.

The chapter also keeps the order straight. This is not the first tool and it is not a magic hack. If you have not done the earlier work, a price pact becomes clownish discipline theater instead of reinforcement.

It also keeps its dignity. The cost is supposed to guard something real, not turn suffering into a hobby. When the price is random or theatrical, the chapter collapses into gimmickry.

That makes identity pacts the right next move. Price is one way to stiffen the spine of a plan; identity changes what kind of person the plan feels attached to.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Chapter 21 argues that distraction often wins because it appears cheaper in the moment than it really is. The skipped block, the opened app, the avoidant detour, or the delayed task all present themselves as low-cost relief while the real damage stays hidden or deferred. That is why Eyal introduces price pacts as a form of precommitment that adds explicit cost before the weak moment begins.

A price pact changes the structure of the choice. The person is no longer deciding only whether to keep the plan. They are also deciding whether to pay a consequence they deliberately accepted when they were thinking clearly. The escape route is no longer falsely free.

The chapter also keeps sequencing central. Price pacts belong after internal-trigger work, traction, and external-trigger redesign. They are not a substitute for earlier methods. They are a last-line support for a plan that already reflects real values.

That is what keeps the chapter from becoming gimmicky. If the reader forgets the order-of-operations rule, explicit cost starts to look like random self-penalty or stunt discipline. The chapter rejects that. The cost should fit the value being protected and should make the weak moment more honest, not more theatrical.

That is also why price pacts are only one subtype. They are useful when distraction keeps pretending to be cheap. But the book still has another way to reinforce prior intent that works through identity rather than explicit cost.

That leads directly to Chapter 22. Once the reader sees what a chosen price can do, the next question is what happens when follow-through is tied to who the person understands themselves to be.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Chapter 21 says price pacts prevent distraction by attaching explicit cost to breaking the plan. A consequence chosen ahead of time corrects the false cheapness of the detour.

This matters because many weak moments are biased toward immediate relief. A price pact changes the moment by adding something concrete the person will lose if they betray prior intent.

The chapter also insists on sequence. Price pacts are not the opening move; they come after earlier methods and protect a plan that already matters. Without that ordering, the chapter turns into gimmickry.

The chapter rejects punishment theater as well. The price should support a genuine value rather than become dramatic suffering for its own sake.

That is why Chapter 22 follows. Cost is one form of reinforcement; identity becomes another.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Chapter 21 catches distraction running one of its oldest scams: the betrayal shows up wearing a discount sticker. Skip the block, dodge the hard thing, drift into the easy thing, and the detour keeps acting like it costs almost nothing. Eyal's answer is simple and ruthless: stop letting the lie ring up at zero. Put a price on the breach before the breach gets a vote.

That changes the moment. You are not just choosing relief over effort anymore. You are choosing whether to pay a consequence you approved while your mind was still honest.

The chapter also keeps the hierarchy straight. This is not the first tool and it is not a carnival trick. If you skip the earlier work, a price pact becomes stunt discipline in a cheap costume.

It also refuses sadism. The price is supposed to defend something real, not convert suffering into a hobby. A bad price pact is random theater. A good one makes the lie of cheap distraction harder to sell.

That is why identity pacts come next. Once the toll booth is standing, the book can ask what happens when the road is guarded not only by cost but by character.
